hints: The cost of a cut depends on how long the piece is at that moment, so the order matters. Think about the first cut on a piece: after it, are the left and right parts independent?
Interval DP over the sorted cut points. Add 0 and length as endpoints; dp[i][j] = cheapest way to make every cut strictly between point i and point j. The first cut in that piece costs p[j] − p[i].

1. Sort the marks and build p = [0, marks…, length].
  2. For gap from 2 upward, for each i (j = i + gap):
  3. dp[i][j] = (p[j] - p[i]) + min over m in (i, j) of dp[i][m] + dp[m][j].
  4. Pieces with no marks inside (gap 1) cost 0.
  5. Return dp[0][last].

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try every order of the cuts (c! permutations) and add up the piece lengths.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Interval DP on the c+2 sorted points, choosing the first cut in each piece.

explain: For a plank of length 8 with marks [2, 5, 6], the points are [0, 2, 5, 6, 8]. Cutting at 5 first costs 8; then the left piece 0–5 is cut at 2 for 5, and the right piece 5–8 is cut at 6 for 3, total 16 — the minimum the DP finds. Choosing the first cut splits the piece into two parts that never affect each other again, which is why the recurrence is correct. Remember to sort the marks; they can come in any order.
recognize: 'Make all the cuts in any order, each cut costs the current piece length' → interval DP over sorted cut points.
